title: Nha Trang food: 6 dishes to try

scenes.narration: Dish one, Ninh Hoa grilled pork. No one knows exactly when it first appeared, but elders in Ninh Hoa say settlers from Thanh Hoa brought the recipe. Lean pork is ground with garlic, pepper, fish sauce and sugar, wrapped around bamboo sticks and grilled over charcoal. The star is a thick dipping sauce simmered from sticky rice, soybean paste, tomato, pork, pig liver, shrimp and peanuts. To eat, roll the pork in crispy fried rice paper with herbs, cucumber, green banana and star fruit, then dip. Try Hong Vu, A Long, or Ba Muoi.
scenes.caption: Nem nướng Ninh Hòa

scenes.narration: Dish two, Nha Trang fish cake noodle soup. This is a seaside city, so the broth is simmered from sea fish and fish bones, clear and light, never greasy. The fish cakes are made from mackerel, barracuda or lizardfish, pounded smooth, then steamed or fried. Add crunchy jellyfish and it becomes bun sua, a bowl you rarely find anywhere else. To eat, add herbs, bean sprouts, chili, a squeeze of lime and a little chili fish sauce. Try Bun Ca seventy nine, Hanh Nhien, or Co Hanh.

scenes.narration: Dish three, banh can, little rice cakes. Their origin is disputed: some sources credit the Cham people of Ninh Thuan, others link them to Da Lat and the Central Highlands. The batter is just rice and water, poured into clay molds over charcoal, topped with quail egg, shrimp or squid, and baked one by one under a lid. To eat, dip them in sweet and sour fish sauce or fermented fish sauce, with shredded green mango and herbs. Go early, many stalls sell only in the morning. Try Ut Lien, Banh Can So Tam, or Co Ly.

scenes.narration: Dish four, goi ca mai, a lime-cured fish salad. No one knows who first made it. Ca mai is a tiny sea fish the size of a thumb, with clear white flesh and no fishy smell. The fish is boned, cured in lime juice or vinegar, then tossed with toasted rice powder, ginger, onion and peanuts. The thick dip is cooked from the fish bones, and some places add pig liver and peanuts. To eat, wrap the fish in rice paper with herbs, green banana, star fruit and cucumber, dip, and enjoy it with grilled rice crackers. Try Goi Ca Ha Ra.

scenes.narration: Dish five, banh canh, a thick rice noodle soup. It is common all over central Vietnam, but Nha Trang is known for versions with fish cake or blue crab, and some shops even use lobster. The chewy noodles are made from rice flour, the broth is simmered with daikon and charred onion, and the fish cakes are fried or steamed. To eat, add scallions, pepper and chili, and dip the fish cake in Khanh Hoa fish sauce with green chili. Try Quan Nho, Co Ba Mien Bien, or Ba Thua.

scenes.narration: Dish six, the last one, Dien Khanh steamed rice sheets. Dien Khanh had an old rice paper craft in Phu Loc village, and over time banh uot kitchens lined the highway, earning it the name banh uot street. Rice is ground into a batter, steamed paper thin, lifted off with bamboo chopsticks, then brushed with scallion oil and sprinkled with shrimp floss and mung beans. To eat, dip it in sweet and sour fish sauce or fermented fish sauce, with pork roll, chili and garlic. Each plate holds just one sheet, so people often eat ten plates. Try Banh Uot Que on 23 October Street.
